title: The angry caller
setting: A customer has been transferred twice and is losing patience.

lines.t: This is the third time I've explained this. Nobody has called me back.
You've told this story three times already, and that's our fault, not yours.
Well. Thank you for saying that.
Let me take ownership of it now. Could you give me your order number?
It's WT four four nine one.
Thank you. I can see it. The delivery is four days late, with no update sent.
So when will it actually arrive?
Thursday is realistic. I could say Wednesday, but I'd rather be honest.
I appreciate that.
I'll send the tracking number now, and I'll call you myself if anything changes.
That's all I wanted from the start, really.

title: A refund request
setting: A customer wants money back outside the returns policy.

lines.t: I'd like a refund. The course wasn't what I expected.
I'm sorry to hear that. May I ask what was different?
I thought it was one to one. It's a group of eight.
I understand. Could I check when you enrolled?
About six weeks ago.
Our returns policy covers thirty days, so a full refund isn't possible.
That's disappointing.
It is. What I can do is move you to the one-to-one track and credit what you've used.
So I'd only pay the difference?
Exactly. Shall I check availability for next month?
Yes, please. That's a fair solution.

title: Between nine and ten
setting: A team lead and an agent look at where the work actually arrives from.

lines.t: Where are the enquiries coming from now?
Half by phone, half by live chat. Chat has doubled since March.
And the call queue in the morning?
Nine to ten is the worst hour of the week. Fourteen people waiting at one point.
What happens out of hours?
They get a message saying we open at eight, and most of them write anyway.
Do we answer those first?
We should. An enquiry sent at eleven at night still expects an answer by nine.
Then move one person from the phones to chat between nine and ten.
That empties the call queue and nobody loses anything. I'll try it on Monday.

title: Don't transfer me again
setting: A customer has already been passed between three people.

lines.t: I've been transferred three times already.
Then I won't transfer a call again today. Tell me the whole thing from the start.
My order never arrived and nobody can say where it is.
I need two minutes with the warehouse. May I put you on hold, or would you prefer a callback?
How long is the callback?
Within the hour, from me, on this number.
Then hold. I don't trust callbacks.
Fair enough. I'll come back every thirty seconds so you know I'm still here.
Nobody has ever done that.
It costs me nothing and it stops you wondering whether the line has died.

title: The number on the wall
setting: Two colleagues work out why good figures and unhappy customers arrive together.

lines.t: Our average wait time is ninety seconds. That's the number on the wall.
And the response time on email?
Four hours, against a service standard of six. We look excellent on paper.
Then why does the satisfaction survey keep saying otherwise?
Because first contact resolution is 48%. Half of them call us twice.
So we answer quickly and solve slowly.
Resolution time is the number nobody put on the wall.
Can we measure it per person?
I'd rather measure it per problem. People aren't the reason the same fault keeps coming back.
Then put resolution time next to wait time and watch what everyone starts doing differently.

title: The second letter
setting: The same customer writes for a second time, angrier than before.

lines.t: Second complaint from the same customer. Same problem, angrier.
What did we say the first time?
That we were sorry and somebody would be in touch.
And was anybody?
No.
So her second letter is really about being ignored.
How do I answer it?
Good complaint handling is boring. Say what happened, say what you'll do, give a date, then do it on that date.
No apology?
One, at the top, in your own words. Then get to the date.

title: The shouting stops
setting: A team lead goes through a difficult call with the agent who took it.

lines.t: He shouted for four minutes. I couldn't get a word in.
You didn't need one. What did you do first?
I let him finish, then said I understood why he was angry.
That's acknowledge and empathise, and it's most of how you de-escalate a difficult customer.
Then he asked who was responsible.
And?
I said I was. I'd rather take ownership than explain our departments to him.
Correct. What did you promise?
Thursday. I think I can do it by Tuesday.
Under-promise and over-deliver, then. Apologise sincerely once, manage expectations honestly, and keep the customer informed even when nothing has moved.

title: Fifteen euros
setting: A part is stuck in Poland and the customer has already waited nine days.

lines.t: I can't resolve this issue today. The part comes from Poland.
What have you told her?
Eleven days. She's already waited nine.
Is there something she can work around in the meantime?
She can use the old one. It's slower.
Then lend her a new one until the part lands. A goodwill gesture worth fifteen euros, on a customer worth four hundred.
Do I escalate the case as well?
Escalate it to the supplier. Inside this building everything is working.
And the case notes?
Write them as though somebody else reads them tomorrow, because somebody will. Don't close the case until the part is in her hands.

title: Fourteen months
setting: A customer brings back something he bought over a year ago.

lines.t: It stopped working. I bought it here fourteen months ago.
Do you have the proof of purchase?
Somewhere. Is it too late?
The warranty runs two years, so no. Our returns policy is thirty days, and a warranty is a separate thing.
Nobody explained that on the phone.
They should have. Would you like a repair, a replacement, or an exchange for the newer model?
What's the difference in price?
An exchange for the same model costs you nothing. The newer one is twenty euros more.
And how long does it take?
A replacement from stock today, if you find that receipt. Check your email, most people buy online and forget.

title: Where is it, actually
setting: Two of three items arrived and nobody told the customer about the third.

lines.t: My order was supposed to arrive on Tuesday.
Can you give me the order number? It starts with two letters.
BG four four one nine.
Thank you. This is a delayed delivery, and I can see exactly why.
Go on.
Two of the three items shipped. The third went out of stock the same morning you ordered.
So where is it now?
On backorder, reaching us on the fourteenth. Nobody told you, and that part is our mistake.
I'd rather have the two now.
They're already moving. Here's the tracking number, and I'll call you myself on the fourteenth.

title: It's her account
setting: A husband calls about his wife's account while she is at work.

lines.t: I'm calling about my wife's account. She's at work all day.
I understand that's inconvenient, and I still have to verify identity before I change anything.
I know her address, her phone number, everything.
The account holder is your wife, so the security question has to be answered by her.
This is ridiculous.
It's the same rule that stops a stranger calling about your account.
Fine. What can you tell me?
That nothing is wrong with the account, and what she'll need when she calls.
Which is?
Two minutes and the answer to one question. I'll put a note on the file so she doesn't start from the beginning.

title: The article nobody could find
setting: Forty calls a month about a setting that is already documented.

lines.t: Forty calls this month about one setting.
There's a knowledge base article about that setting. I wrote it.
Then why is the phone ringing?
Because it's called 'Configuration parameters' and nobody searches for that.
What would they search for?
'Change my email address'. That's what they actually want.
Rename it, then. What about the FAQ page?
Eleven questions, and four of them nobody has ever asked.
Replace those four with the four we answer every day.
Then self-service works for the people who prefer it, and the phone is free for the people who don't.

title: Six years, then nothing
setting: A customer who ordered every month for six years stopped in January.

lines.t: She ordered every month for six years, then stopped in January.
Did anyone ask her why?
Nobody. We only send the feedback form after a complaint.
So we hear from the angry ones and never from the ones who quietly leave.
Call her.
And say what? 'Come back'?
Ask what changed. A loyal customer who leaves usually has one specific reason and will tell you in a sentence.
And if the reason is us?
Then you've learned something worth more than the order. You win back a customer by fixing the thing. A discount only delays the next goodbye.
I'll call her, and the other eleven repeat customers who stopped this year.
